description: We're Astrovex, a team driven by space exploration and the tech that brings it closer to everyone. We blend graphic design, web development, animation, and AI/ML to turn complex space data into immersive, intuitive experiences. We're looking for teammates skilled in data analysis, visualization, coding, or storytelling, and above all, curious and driven. Join Astrovex and let's build something out of this world!
summary:
## NASA FLAME INTELLIGENCE PLATFORM
**From Microgravity Experiments to Autonomous Fire Safety Intelligence**

NASA Flame Intelligence Platform is an AI-powered scientific research platform that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion research into actionable fire safety intelligence for future space exploration. It integrates authorised NASA research resources and experimental data to explore combustion behaviour, compare investigations and identify relationships between oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuels and materials.

Using a multi-agent AI architecture, scientific knowledge extraction, evidence-based retrieval and interactive data visualisations, the platform helps researchers discover relevant experiments, interpret findings and identify research gaps. Its predictive analytics and interactive Moon and Mars habitat simulator explore fire safety scenarios while distinguishing actual experimental measurements from model predictions and hypothetical conditions.

By connecting decades of combustion research with intelligent scientific analysis, our solution supports better-informed fire prevention, detection and suppression strategies. This is important because understanding how fire behaves in microgravity and different atmospheric conditions is essential to protecting astronauts, spacecraft and future lunar and Martian habitats.
details:
1. What it does and how it works

The platform turns NASA's microgravity combustion record into an auditable research workspace rather than a chatbot over documents. It works in four layers:

Inspection layer. A bootstrap job visits the 13 authorised NASA records (10 PSI investigations — FLEX, FLEX-2, BASS, BASS-II, SAME, SAME-R, SAFFIRE-I/II, ACME BRE, ACME s-Flame — plus 3 Spinoff technology-transfer records), records an HTTP receipt, SHA-256 hash, content type, byte count and extraction progress for each, and writes NASA_RESOURCE_AUDIT.md + NASA_RESOURCE_MANIFEST.json.

Ingestion and retrieval. Fetched pages are decoded, text-extracted (HTML and PDF via PyMuPDF), chunked, entity-linked to investigations and materials, and indexed. Retrieval is in-process BM25/TF-IDF (swappable for pgvector on Postgres), so every answer returns the chunk_id and resource it came from.

Nine-agent orchestrator. Discovery → Inspection → Extraction → Research Intelligence → Fire Safety → Predictive Analytics → Investigation Ranking → Validation → Report. Each agent is a deterministic Python callable — an LLM writes prose only, never state — and every step is persisted to the database while it runs, so the UI shows a genuine trace instead of an animation pretending to be work.

Workspace. 15 authenticated modules: mission overview, resource audit centre, ingestion control, research assistant with citations, knowledge graph, evidence ledger, agent network, ranking, predictive scenario modelling, data explorer, safety brief, PDF reports, audit ledger, settings, shell. Login uses HMAC-SHA256 bearer tokens with scrypt password hashing and role gates (viewer / researcher / lead).

Scenario model. A transparent screening model combines oxygen partial pressure, a material flammability baseline (LOI), a microgravity residence-time correction, a forced-flow correction and a suppressant-efficacy term into a 0–100 hazard index. It ships with a published model card, its coefficients and its limitations. It is explicitly not a NASA model.

2. Benefits

  • Traceability over fluency. Any claim can be walked back to a chunk, a resource, an HTTP receipt and a hash. Orphan claims fail validation.
  • Honest degradation. Ten PSI pages are client-rendered Angular shells (~950 bytes of placeholder HTML). The pipeline detects this, marks those records PARTIAL, states that rendered field values could not be verified server-side, and labels the curated text it substitutes at reduced confidence (0.62 vs 0.86) instead of pretending the scrape succeeded.
  • Separation of evidence from inference. Eight evidence labels — NASA DOCUMENTED FINDING, REDUCED CONFIDENCE, AI INTERPRETATION, MODEL PREDICTION, HYPOTHETICAL SCENARIO, HISTORICAL INCIDENT, INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE, and curated metadata — are enforced in the API and rendered in the UI and PDFs. Where the corpus cannot support a number (e.g. detection time), the platform returns INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE rather than a plausible-looking guess.
  • Reproducible audits. Re-inspecting a resource writes a new receipt and ledger entry, so drift in a source over time is visible.
  • Operational, not just analytic. Recommendations are dispatchable actions ("Re-inspect FLEX-2", "Review 17 reduced-confidence claims") that run real endpoints and log what happened.

3. Intended impact

Fire safety in spacecraft is a low-data, high-consequence domain: you cannot run a large fire test on a crewed vehicle, so decisions rest on a small set of flight experiments. The project's aim is to make that small evidence base queryable, auditable and defensible — for mission planners sizing habitat atmospheres and materials, for researchers identifying where the evidence actually stops, and for reviewers who need to see why a recommendation was made. The demo target is a lunar-habitat fire-safety review: what do FLEX, BASS and SAFFIRE actually establish, where is the corpus silent, and what would we test next.

A second, general impact is methodological: it demonstrates a pattern for evidence-bounded AI in safety-critical science — deterministic state, retrieval-grounded prose, published model cards, and a refusal path built into the architecture rather than bolted on as a disclaimer.

4. Tools, languages and software

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS; Framer Motion and GSAP for motion; Three.js + React Three Fiber/drei for the GLSL flame, knowledge graph and habitat scenes; Recharts for data; lucide-react icons.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2, SQLite (Postgres/pgvector-ready), httpx, BeautifulSoup/lxml, PyMuPDF, hashlib/hmac/scrypt for receipts and auth. PDF reports use a dependency-free writer.
  • Optional: an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint for prose synthesis — server-side only, never in the browser. Without a key the assistant runs identical extractive retrieval with the same citations.
  • Data: NASA PSI (psi.nasa.gov) and NASA Spinoff (spinoff.nasa.gov) records only; no other external research source is reachable from the pipeline.
  • Deployment: Cloudflare Workers (site hosting + /api proxy), Vercel Python serverless functions for the API, bundled SQLite corpus snapshot copied to a writable /tmp at cold start.
  • Hardware: none beyond commodity hardware — intentionally, so the platform can run where mission teams already work.

5. Creativity

  • The audit as the interface. Instead of hiding the scraper, the platform promotes the HTTP receipt, hash, extracted character count and recorded limitation to first-class UI. Integrity checks become a dashboard, not a footnote.
  • A flame that is a rendering, not a claim. The hero visual is custom GLSL with additive glow and an instanced particle field, explicitly annotated as visualisation; the 3D habitat is labelled schematic, with subsystem readouts marked as the scenario values the user typed, not simulated telemetry.
  • Agents you can audit. The agent network lights up from real AgentStep rows, so what looks like motion design is actually execution state.
  • Two registers. A cinematic scroll-told landing page for the argument, and a dense instrumentation-style workspace for the work — same data, same labels, different rhetorical mode.
  • Refusal as a feature. "0 of 4 query terms appear in the authorised corpus" is a designed answer, presented with the missing terms named, rather than a low-confidence fabrication.

6. Factors considered

  • Hallucination risk. Deterministic agents, retrieval-only answers, citations on every claim, model outputs quarantined behind a model card and a not_a_nasa_model flag.
  • Client-rendered sources. Rather than adding a headless browser to manufacture completeness, the limitation is recorded and confidence is reduced.
  • Data provenance and IP. Only 13 named, public NASA URLs are permitted; validation fails if a foreign URL enters the registry. Historical incidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) are kept in a separate table so accident narratives never masquerade as experimental data.
  • Scientific honesty in visualisation. Every chart is an aggregation of retrieved metadata; nothing is a synthetic measurement series. The trend chart is labelled cross-sectional, because a trend over time would require repeated audits.
  • Accessibility. prefers-reduced-motion is honoured globally plus a per-account switch; 3D scenes fall back to static representations; safety status is written in words as well as colour.
  • Security and cost. Server-side secrets only, role-gated mutations, scrypt hashing, LLM strictly optional so the platform runs with no API key.
  • Known limitations, stated deliberately: the hosted API's /tmp store is ephemeral, so runtime notes and re-inspections do not persist across instances; the scenario model is a screening tool with no flame geometry; no automated test suite is shipped — verification was typecheck, build, bootstrap/report smoke runs and live API checks.

Not an official NASA product. Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 brief "Flame in Freefall: AI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion."
